name: HTTP Caching Headers
intent: Use the HTTP protocol's own rules (Cache-Control, validators, Vary, Age) so browsers and shared caches know exactly when they may reuse a response.
scenario: A shop has an HTML page, a CSS/JS bundle, a products API response and a per-user profile, served through a CDN (a network of shared caches close to users). Alice and Bob visit every minute and a new version is deployed at minute 4. Which headers make Alice see the new site at once, keep the bundle cached for a year, and never show Bob Alice's profile?
problem: A response can be reused by the browser, by a CDN, by a corporate proxy, or by nobody, and each of them decides from the response headers alone. Too little caching wastes bandwidth and round trips. Too much caching leaves users on an old page you cannot fix, or serves one user's private data to another. The headers are the only contract: you cannot reach into a user's browser and delete a copy.

howItWorks.title: Freshness: how long a stored response may be reused without asking
howItWorks.text: The freshness lifetime comes from Cache-Control: max-age=N (seconds), or s-maxage=N for shared caches only (it overrides max-age there and is ignored by browsers). A response is fresh while its age is below the lifetime, where age = the Age header the previous cache reported + the time spent in this cache. Without any of these, a cache with a Last-Modified header may guess (heuristic freshness): typically 10% of the time since Last-Modified, so a file last changed 10 days ago may be reused for a day with no header at all.

howItWorks.title: Validation: asking cheaply instead of downloading again
howItWorks.text: When a response is stale (or marked no-cache) the cache sends a conditional request: If-None-Match: "etag" (from the stored ETag, a version label the server puts on each response) or If-Modified-Since: <Last-Modified>. If the resource is unchanged, the origin answers 304 Not Modified with no body (a few hundred bytes), and the cache refreshes the stored copy and resets its age. If it changed, it answers 200 with the new body and the new validator. ETag is more reliable than Last-Modified, which has one-second granularity.

howItWorks.title: The directives that change the rules
howItWorks.text: no-cache means store it but revalidate before every reuse. no-store means never write it anywhere. private means only the browser may store it (not a CDN or proxy); public explicitly allows shared storage, for example for responses to requests with an Authorization header. must-revalidate forbids serving it stale once expired. immutable says it will never change during its lifetime, so even a reload need not revalidate. stale-while-revalidate=N (RFC 5861) serves the stale copy instantly for N more seconds while refreshing in the background; stale-if-error=N serves stale if the origin returns 5xx or is unreachable.

howItWorks.title: Cache keys and Vary
howItWorks.text: A cache stores a response under its URL (and method). Vary lists request headers that also select the stored variant: Vary: Accept-Encoding keeps a gzip and a br copy apart, which is cheap because only a few values exist. Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent fragments the cache into near-unique entries, so the hit rate collapses; and omitting Vary on a personalised response makes the cache serve one variant to everyone. Personal data should instead be marked private, no-cache or no-store.

howItWorks.title: Cache busting: change the URL, not the headers
howItWorks.text: Static assets get a content hash in the file name (app.3f9a1c.js) and Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. A new build produces a new URL, so the old entries are simply never requested again, and a year-long lifetime is safe. The HTML that references the hashed names is the one entry point you cannot rename, so it is served with no-cache (or a short max-age with stale-while-revalidate) and validated on every visit.

howItWorks.title: How a reload changes the request
howItWorks.text: A normal navigation uses fresh stored copies. A normal reload (F5) revalidates the page itself with a conditional request, while its subresources are still reused if fresh. A hard reload (Ctrl+Shift+R) sends Cache-Control: no-cache without validators for the page and everything it loads, so every layer must go back to the origin (a CDN can still answer by revalidating its own copy). Users do this when your cache headers are wrong; do not rely on it.

pros: Fresh hits cost 0 bytes and 0 round trips, and ETag revalidation turns a 400 KB download into a roughly 300 byte 304
It is a standard every browser, CDN and proxy already implements, so it works without any code in the client
Hashed file names with a one-year lifetime remove most static traffic and make deploys atomic
stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error hide revalidation latency and short outages from users
cons: You cannot invalidate a copy already sitting in a user's browser: a long max-age on a mutable URL is a decision you cannot undo until it expires
Every layer applies the rules independently, and the Age header makes the remaining freshness at the browser shorter than you configured
The directive vocabulary is easy to misread (no-cache versus no-store, s-maxage versus max-age), and misreading it either leaks data or wastes the cache
no-cache and short lifetimes still cost a round trip per resource on every visit, which hurts on slow mobile links
whenToUse: Versioned static assets (hashed file names): max-age=31536000, immutable
HTML and other mutable documents: no-cache with an ETag, or a short max-age plus stale-while-revalidate
Read-mostly API responses where a bounded delay is acceptable: a short max-age or s-maxage, with an ETag
Personal or authenticated responses that should be reused only by that user's browser: private, plus no-cache or a very short max-age
whenNotToUse: Responses that must never be written to disk, such as bank statements, tokens or one-time pages: use no-store, accepting that nothing is reused
State that has to be read-your-writes consistent right after an update: caching headers cannot tell a browser that something changed, so fetch it with no-cache or a versioned URL
As a way to protect data: private and no-store are instructions to well-behaved caches, not access control
Tiny responses on a fast network where a 304 round trip costs as much as the body: complexity with no benefit
pitfalls: Serving the HTML page with a long max-age (or only a Last-Modified header, so heuristic freshness applies): after a deploy users keep the old page, and its references to old assets, for as long as the lifetime lasts
Believing no-cache means do not cache: it means revalidate before reuse. The one that forbids storing is no-store, and using no-store on assets throws away every 304
Putting a user's data behind a CDN without private or no-store: the CDN keys on the URL, so the first user's profile is served to the next one
Vary: Cookie (or Vary: User-Agent) on a public resource: every distinct cookie creates its own cache entry and the hit rate drops to near zero; strip the cookie or mark the response private instead
Sending Last-Modified with no Cache-Control and assuming nothing is cached: browsers and CDNs apply heuristic freshness (about 10% of the age since Last-Modified)
A hashed file name on the bundle but a cached HTML page that still references the old hash: the user stays on the old build
Different ETags from each server behind a load balancer (for example ones derived from inode numbers) so 304s never match and conditional requests become full downloads

roles.label: Browser cache
roles.description: A private cache: one user's copy of each response, applying max-age and sending conditional requests.

roles.label: Shared cache (CDN)
roles.description: Stores responses for many users, honours s-maxage and private, and adds an Age header to what it serves.

roles.label: Origin server
roles.description: Decides the headers, the ETag and whether a conditional request gets a 304 or a new body.

quiz.question: Your site's HTML page references app.js and app.css with hashed names, and a new deploy changes the hashes. Users should see each deploy on their next visit, but you also want an unchanged page to cost only a tiny response. Which header on the HTML best fits?
options: Cache-Control: max-age=86400, since the hashed assets already handle updates
Cache-Control: no-store, so no browser or CDN ever holds an old copy
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, because the HTML rarely changes
Cache-Control: no-cache, together with an ETag so unchanged pages return 304
quiz.explanation: no-cache means store the page but revalidate before each reuse, so a changed page is picked up at once and an unchanged one costs a small 304. A long max-age pins users to the old HTML and its old asset names, while no-store throws away the 304 saving.

quiz.question: A CDN sits in front of your API. To speed up GET /api/me, which returns the signed-in user's profile, a developer wants each user's browser to reuse the response for 60 seconds. It must never be stored by the CDN. Which header does this?
quiz.explanation: private lets only the user's own browser store it, with a 60 second lifetime. public and s-maxage invite the CDN to key on the URL and hand the first user's profile to the next, while no-store gives no browser reuse at all.

quiz.question: A public product page is identical for everyone, but the app sets a tracking cookie on every visitor and someone added Vary: Cookie to the response. The CDN hit ratio fell from 90% to 3%. What is the best fix?
options: Raise max-age to a full day so each cookie-specific entry stays in the cache for longer
Remove Vary: Cookie and strip the cookie from the cache key, as the page is not personalised
Switch to Vary: User-Agent, which has fewer distinct values than cookies and would still protect users
Change the response to no-cache so the CDN revalidates each cookie variant instead of refetching it in full
quiz.explanation: Vary: Cookie gives every visitor a near-unique cache entry, so almost every request misses. If the body does not depend on the cookie, it should not be in the cache key. Vary: User-Agent also has very many values, and a longer lifetime or no-cache does not make the entries shareable.
